meta.description: One book, no corroboration. The line appears in John J. O'Neill's Prodigal Genius: The Life of Nikola Tesla (1944), unsourced. Tesla's own 1919 memoir mentions the $50,000 'practical joke' but never names Edison and never quotes the remark.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You don't understand our American humor'?
meta.ogDescription: The Edison–Tesla insult everyone knows rests on a single 1944 biography that gives no source. Tesla's own account blames 'the Manager' and quotes nobody.

answer.label: Attributed to Edison by one 1944 book — and nothing else
answer.sourceLine: The whole story rests on one book: John J. O’Neill’s Prodigal Genius: The Life of Nikola Tesla, published in 1944, the year after Tesla died. O’Neill gives no source for the remark — no letter, no interview, no witness — and there the trail ends. What survives independently is Tesla’s own account in his 1919 memoir, and it is notably different: he says ‘the Manager’ promised him $50,000, that it ‘turned out to be a practical joke,’ and he neither names Edison nor quotes anybody.

source.excerpt: The Manager had promised me $50,000 on the completion of this task but it turned out to be a practical joke. This gave me a painful shock and I resigned my position.
trail: Every retelling — Wikipedia, the comics, the YouTube explainers — runs back to the same place: O’Neill’s Prodigal Genius (1944). O’Neill was a Pulitzer-winning science journalist who had known Tesla for years, which is why the book is taken seriously. But for this scene he cites nothing, and no earlier printing of the line has ever been found the investigation ↗.

Tesla told the story himself, twenty-five years earlier, in My Inventions (1919). His version is the excerpt above. It contains the $50,000 and the ‘practical joke’ — and it attributes the promise to ‘the Manager,’ not to Edison, and quotes no reply at all.

The gap between the two accounts is where the famous line lives. Somebody had to turn Tesla’s anonymous manager into Edison and supply him with a sneer, and the earliest text that does both is O’Neill’s.

Two further wrinkles worth knowing. Tesla’s own memoir is not perfectly reliable either — he says he worked there ‘nearly a year’ when the documented span is around six months. And Samuel Insull, then Edison’s business manager, is a more plausible candidate for ‘the Manager’ than Edison himself.
source.excerptNote: Tesla’s own words, published in Electrical Experimenter in 1919 — the closest thing to a primary document, and the reason the underlying grievance is real. Read it for what it does not say. No Edison, no dialogue, no American humor. Just a manager, a broken promise and a resignation.

source.rightsNote: We are not giving a rights status for this one, because it depends on a US copyright renewal we have not checked. O’Neill’s Prodigal Genius was published in 1944 and O’Neill died in 1953; American books of that vintage are protected only if their copyright was renewed in the 1970s, and the book circulates widely online as though it were free. Tesla’s own 1919 memoir, quoted above, is comfortably public domain. Safest course: quote Tesla’s 1919 sentence freely, and treat the O’Neill scene as protected until you have checked the renewal records. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Thomas Edison
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Edison
author.bio: Thomas Edison is the designated villain of the Tesla story, and this line is the moment the villainy is supposed to be established — a sneer that is both a swindle and an ethnic slight against a young immigrant engineer. It is a very good scene. That is part of the problem: it is exactly the sentence a biographer writing a sympathetic life of Tesla in 1944 would want to exist. Edison was a hard commercial operator, and Tesla’s grievance about the money is genuine and documented in his own hand. The quotation is not.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is a one-book case, and saying so precisely is the whole point. Nobody has proved the line is invented. What can be shown is that every trace of it descends from a single unsourced page, published the year after the only other witness died.

items.why: Prodigal Genius gives the scene — Tesla builds the machines, asks for the $50,000, is laughed at — and cites nothing for it. O’Neill knew Tesla personally, so he may well have had it from him. He may also have dramatised Tesla’s written account. There is no way to tell, and no second source to check him against the trail ↗.

My Inventions (1919): ‘The Manager had promised me $50,000… but it turned out to be a practical joke.’ That is Tesla, in print, twenty-five years earlier, with every incentive to name Edison — and he does not. Nor does he quote a reply.

Samuel Insull ran the business side of Edison’s operation and fits Tesla’s description better than Edison does. The $50,000 figure is also hard to credit — it would have been more than the Machine Works could plausibly hand a junior engineer, and would have made Tesla wealthy overnight.

The memoir says he worked there ‘nearly a year’; the record says about six months. And the documented trigger for his resignation was a disagreement over a different invention. Correcting O’Neill does not mean promoting Tesla’s account to gospel.

misattribution.truthLine: The words exist in exactly one place: an unsourced page of a 1944 biography. Tesla’s own account of the same episode names no one and quotes no one the investigation ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is the perfect origin story for a rivalry that people badly want to have happened: the immigrant genius does the work, the American showman keeps the money and laughs at him for not getting the joke. Everything the modern Tesla myth needs is compressed into eight words.

Which is precisely why it deserves the scrutiny. A quotation that is this useful to one side of an argument, and that appears for the first time in a book written by that side’s advocate the year after the last witness died, has earned a raised eyebrow.
context.detailsSummary: What is documented and what is not
detailsBody: Documented: Tesla worked at the Edison Machine Works in New York from 1884, for around six months, redesigning dynamos.
Documented: in My Inventions (1919) Tesla writes that ‘the Manager’ promised him $50,000, that it proved a practical joke, and that he resigned.
Not documented: that the manager was Edison.
Not documented: that anybody said ‘You don’t understand our American humor.’
First appearance of both claims: John J. O’Neill, Prodigal Genius, 1944, with no source given.
Everything since — encyclopaedias, comics, documentaries — is downstream of that one page.
